contraindications: Propranolol: asthma, second- or third-degree heart block, marked bradycardia, uncontrolled heart failure.
Topiramate: pregnancy; in a woman who can become pregnant only with highly effective contraception under the pregnancy prevention programme (MHRA 2024).
Amitriptyline: recent myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, heart block.
output.formulary_status: Propranolol, candesartan, amitriptyline, topiramate: on formulary.
interactions: Propranolol, candesartan or topiramate with sumatriptan: no clinically significant interaction (the propranolol dose adjustment applies to rizatriptan, not sumatriptan).
Amitriptyline with sumatriptan: both serotonergic; serotonin syndrome is rare; counsel on symptoms.
Candesartan with NSAIDs: reduced antihypertensive effect and risk of renal impairment with regular use.
Paracetamol: no interaction with any of the four.
output.proposed: Migraine preventive options: propranolol, candesartan, amitriptyline, topiramate. Current: sumatriptan, paracetamol
output.summary: None of the four preventives interacts significantly with sumatriptan or paracetamol; candesartan and topiramate need pregnancy safeguards, topiramate under the pregnancy prevention programme. Sources: SmPCs, BNF, MHRA Drug Safety Update 2024.
warnings: Topiramate: paraesthesia, cognitive slowing and word-finding difficulty, weight loss, kidney stones, metabolic acidosis, rarely acute angle-closure glaucoma; reduces the efficacy of oral contraceptive pills at higher doses.
Propranolol: fatigue, cold extremities, sleep disturbance, depression; reduced exercise tolerance.
Amitriptyline: sedation, dry mouth, constipation, weight gain.
Candesartan: dizziness and hypotension at start; check renal function and potassium.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Seven years of identical attacks, 2-4 a month; visual aura spreading over 20-25 minutes, then migraine headache with vomiting; 5 of 6 C characteristics; MIDAS 24; normal examination, no red flag; acute-medication days below overuse thresholds
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache/aura history, neurological examination and red-flag review; apply every ICHD-3 1.2 criterion explicitly
action_criteria.rationale: The structured history confirms ICHD-3 1.2.1, counts headache and acute-medication days (episodic, no overuse) and records the disability that sets the preventive decision; no red flag calls for imaging.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4; offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.
Do not offer valproate for migraine prevention: she can become pregnant (MHRA 2024).
required_recommendations: Diagnose migraine with typical aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1), episodic, with severe disability (MIDAS 24, grade IV); no imaging is needed.

Start preventive treatment (2-4 severe attacks a month with MIDAS grade IV meet the AHS 2021 threshold): for example propranolol modified-release 80 mg daily titrated to 160 mg (after checking for asthma, depression and bradycardia), or amitriptyline, or candesartan (only with reliable contraception, as it is contraindicated in pregnancy); review after 8-12 weeks with a headache diary.

If topiramate is chosen, start it only with highly effective contraception (copper or hormonal IUD, or implant) under the topiramate pregnancy prevention programme; it reduces the efficacy of oral and progestogen-only pills.

Acute plan: sumatriptan 50-100 mg with naproxen 500 mg or paracetamol at headache onset, an antiemetic such as metoclopramide 10 mg for the vomiting, prescribed in a quantity that covers her attacks; keep triptan use under 10 days a month.

If oral preventives fail or are not tolerated, consider a CGRP monoclonal antibody: the EHF 2022 guideline supports it after two failed oral preventives, and NICE funding requires at least three failed preventives and at least 4 migraine days a month [Sacco_2022].

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential
EEG is not indicated for migraine with aura; reserve for cases where focal seizure is genuinely on the differential

accepted: Established migraine with typical visual aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1), MIDAS grade IV — preventive therapy indicated

differential.key_features: Excluded as the main diagnosis: every attack has a stereotyped, gradually spreading visual aura
Excluded by the attack count: 2-4 attacks a month, far below 15 headache days
Acute medication on about 4-6 days a month (sumatriptan up to 4, paracetamol): below the 10-day triptan and 15-day simple-analgesic thresholds
Throbbing unilateral headache with vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia after an aura is migrainous

key_clinical_evidence: Seven years of stereotyped visual aura followed by migraine headache meet ICHD-3 1.2.1; normal examination and no red flag, so no imaging is needed.
Two to four severe attacks a month with vomiting and MIDAS 24 (grade IV) are episodic migraine with severe disability: preventive treatment is indicated (AHS 2021) and has never been offered.
She can become pregnant: valproate is not used, topiramate only under the pregnancy prevention programme, candesartan stopped before conception.

findings.result: Stereotyped attacks since age 27 (7 years), 2-4 a month; no change in character.

Visual only: shimmering spot near central vision expanding into a zigzag flickering crescent in one hemifield, side alternating between attacks; fully reversible. No sensory, speech, motor or brainstem symptoms.
Predominantly unilateral throbbing headache, 7-9/10, begins as the aura fades; nausea, vomiting 1-2 times per attack, photophobia, phonophobia; lasts 8-16 hours; goes to bed in a dark room.

Sumatriptan 50 mg effective, up to 4 days a month (supply runs out); paracetamol 1000 mg on the remaining attack days. Acute-medication days about 4-6 a month: below medication-overuse thresholds. Zolmitriptan previously, similar effect. No preventive ever tried.
Normal: full visual fields to confrontation, no papilloedema on fundoscopy, normal power, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait.

Systemic symptoms: absent. Neoplasia or immunosuppression: absent. Neurological deficit outside the aura: absent. Sudden or thunderclap onset: absent. Onset after 50: absent (onset at 27). Pattern change: absent. Positional or Valsalva trigger: absent. Papilloedema: absent. Pregnancy: absent. Painful eye: absent. Medication overuse: absent.

clinical_assessment.impression: ICHD-3 1.2.1 criteria met: recurrent fully reversible visual aura with 5 of 6 criterion C characteristics, followed by migraine headache. Episodic pattern (2-4 attacks a month) with severe disability (MIDAS grade IV). No SNNOOP10 red flag.

scores.ICHD-3 criterion C characteristics met: 5 of 6 (at least 3 required): spread, duration, unilateral, positive, headache within 60 min; no succession

patient.history_present_illness:
A 34-year-old Jamaican-British woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic requesting a management review for her long-standing migraine with aura. She has experienced episodic visual disturbances followed by headache since age 27. She describes a consistent pattern: a small shimmering spot appears near her central vision, then slowly expands into a bright, arc-shaped crescent of zigzag flickering light over approximately 20-25 minutes. The aura affects one side of her vision, though she says it alternates sides between episodes. As the aura fades, she develops a moderate-to-severe throbbing headache (7-9/10) that is predominantly unilateral, accompanied by nausea, vomiting (1-2 episodes/attack), photophobia, and phonophobia, lasting 8-16 hours. She has 2-4 episodes per month and typically needs to go to bed in a darkened room.

She currently manages acute attacks with sumatriptan 50 mg which she has used for 2 years with good effect, but notes she runs out of tablets most months. She previously tried zolmitriptan with similar efficacy. She has never tried preventive medication. She is a primary school teacher, finds attacks very disruptive to her professional life (missing school days, difficulty planning), and scores 24 on the MIDAS questionnaire (grade IV, severe disability). She has no cardiac disease, no hypertension, and no prior TIA or stroke. She is not on any contraception (partner had vasectomy). Non-smoker. Her mother and older sister both have migraines.
